blocks: In this garden, Year pages model a period of calendar time named by digits: a single year, or — when the garden wants to attach content to the whole span — its decade or century.
Year — one calendar year; the primary sense of this type.
Decade — the ten years sharing every digit but the last.
Century — the hundred years sharing every digit but the last two.

Not this type: a specific day, which is a Logseq/Entity/Time/Date instance, or a month, which stays a plain date wikilink per Logseq/Date, or a named historical era without a numeral (e.g. "the Renaissance") — model that as Logseq/Entity/Concept instead.
Naming — digit groups, most significant first
A year's canonical page splits its four digits into groups, most significant first: <century>/<decade digit>/<year digit>, e.g. 19/5/9 for 1959.
Naming — digit groups, most significant first
Its decade page drops the last segment: for the 1950s. Its century page drops the last two: 19 for 1900-1999.
Naming — digit groups, most significant first

This is the same grouping Logseq/Date already uses for older dates (e.g. for 1749); this entity extends it to every year, so all three granularities cluster together and sort in true chronological order regardless of era.
Naming — digit groups, most significant first
Every instance takes the plain numeral as its alias::: 1959 for the year, 1950s for the decade, 1900-1999 for the century.
Logseq/Date governs which literal text to type inline for a date value (e.g. prefer typing [[1959]] for a post-1900 year); the alias resolves that text to the same canonical page either way.
Derive the digit-group path from the numeral and check whether that page already exists before creating it.
A decade or century page is created only when something wants to attach to that whole span — a year does not require its decade or century parent to exist first.
Set logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Time/Year]] on year, decade, and century pages alike.
alias:: carries the plain numeral, per above.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Frontmatter alone (logseq-entity:: and alias::) is a complete instance.
Body content is optional and, when present, covers what makes that particular year, decade, or century notable.

Logseq/Date governs how date values appear as wikilink text. This entity models the pages that text can point to, including the decade and century granularities Logseq/Date does not itself define a wikilink form for.

Any entity in the garden that has a known creation year — a book, a movie, a podcast episode, an essay, a musical composition, a work of art, and so on — may carry logseq-created-time-year:: pointing at the year, decade, or century instance that matches what is actually known.

This is separate from that entity's own date-created::, which may hold a more precise value (or, on older pages, may already be this same grouped link). Setting both is normal; logseq-created-time-year:: is what makes the creation year a queryable, backlinked relationship regardless of which entity type carries it.
Full property definition: Logseq/Frontmatter/logseq-created-time-year. Pages that still need this link backfilled are tracked at Logseq/Entity/Time/Year/Todos.

Pages whose date-created:: already resolves to a specific year, decade, or century but do not yet carry logseq-created-time-year::, per the precedent recorded on Logseq/Entity/Time/Year.
This is a first pass over pages whose date-created:: value is already year-only (or the older grouped form) — not yet a full sweep of every page carrying a day- or month-precision date.

In this garden, Trade-Off pages model a tension among several choices, where taking more of one means taking less of another, explained one choice at a time.

Two or more choices that pull against each other, so that deciding means choosing how far to lean toward each. The page explains what each choice gains, what it gives up, and how the balance gets struck.
The number of choices is open. Two is the common case, three or four read fine, and the shape holds to about ten. Past that the page is a catalog of options, and Logseq/Entity/Collection fits better.
Not a Trade-Off: a pair of look-alike ideas told apart, such as Knowledge/Concept/Knowledge Base vs Knowledge Garden; a feature comparison of tools; a Logseq/Entity/Question.
A Trade-Off is understanding-oriented writing, so every instance also declares Logseq/Entity/Concept, Concept first: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Concept]], [[Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off]].
The path joins the choices with a vs segment: X/vs/Y, and with more choices X/vs/Y/vs/Z. Order the choices the way the tension is spoken: Explore before Exploit, Risk before Reward.

Place the page in the topic namespace where the tension is discussed when the garden has one, as with AI/Concept/Explore/vs/Exploit. A tension with no home topic sits at the root, as with Risk/vs/Reward.
alias:: carries the spoken form with the type as a suffix: X vs Y Trade-Off.
Frontmatter — alias:: as above; logseq-entity:: with Concept first, then this page; see-also:: for related pages the body does not mention.
H1 — the choices joined with vs, each linked to its standalone page when the garden has one: - # [[Explore]] vs [[Exploit]].
## Summary — what is being traded and why the choices pull against each other, in a paragraph or two.
## The Trade-Off — one H3 per choice. The heading links the choice's Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off/Component page, and that page is embedded beneath it, as on AI/Concept/Explore/vs/Exploit:
Further H2 sections as the topic warrants, drawing on the Logseq/Entity/Concept shape: how the balance is struck in practice, where the tension came from, examples.
Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off/Component — one page per choice, filed under the trade-off page and embedded into it.
Logseq/Entity/Concept — the primary type of every Trade-Off page.

Logseq/Entity/Term — a choice often has its own standalone page, such as Explore or Exploit. That page defines the thing in general; the component page explains it inside this one tension and points back with see-also::.

Search each choice's name, the vs path in either order, and existing Logseq/Entity/Concept pages with vs in the title. One page per tension. A Concept page that already explains the tension takes this type in addition, with its body reshaped to match.
In this garden, Trade-Off Component pages model one choice inside a Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off, explained in the context of that tension.
One of the choices a trade-off page weighs. The page says what leaning toward this choice gains, what it gives up, and what leaning too far looks like.

The component stays scoped to its trade-off. The thing itself may have a standalone page in the garden, such as Exploit, and may be a component of other trade-offs as well; each component page explains the choice inside one tension only.
One segment under the trade-off page, repeating the choice's name from the path: X/vs/Y/X and X/vs/Y/Y; with more choices, X/vs/Y/vs/Z/Z.
see-also:: — the standalone page for the thing itself first, when the garden has one, then other pages that explain this choice.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
The page renders inside its trade-off's ## The Trade-Off section through a page embed, under an H3 that already names it, so the body starts with the choice itself and skips the H1.
Lean bullets: what choosing this means inside the tension; what it gains; what it costs; what too much of it looks like.
Logseq/Entity/Trade-Off — the page that weighs this choice against the others and embeds this page.
Logseq/Entity/Term and Logseq/Entity/Concept — where the thing itself is defined or explained in general, linked from see-also::.
In this garden, UI Area pages model one named region of a product's interface — a panel section on hardware, or a view or bar in software — and list the controls and smaller areas inside it.
A region the product's own documentation names and that holds controls: Microfreak/UI/Oscillator, Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View.
<Item>/UI is the root area for an item and covers its whole interface, the way <Item>/UG holds its Logseq/Entity/Book/User Guide.
A single knob, button, pad or field is a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control, not an area.
A small group of controls stays a heading on its area page rather than becoming a page, even when the documentation names it, such as the Transport Controls section of Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar.
A UI Area corresponds to an UX/Design/Atomic/L3 - Organism; a root <Item>/UI page or a full view such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View corresponds to an UX/Design/Atomic/L4 - Template.

A Logseq/Entity/UI/Control corresponds to an UX/Design/Atomic/L1 - Atom. A preset or a saved Live Set, which fills the interface with real values, corresponds to an UX/Design/Atomic/L5 - Page and is modeled by its own entity.
Place an area at <Item>/UI/<Area>, nesting a smaller area under the area that holds it: <Item>/UI/<Area>/<Sub-area>.

A hardware panel can also be mapped by position. Each side of the device is an area, <Item>/UI/Front or <Item>/UI/Rear; a side laid out in rows has one area per row at <Item>/UI/Front/Row/<NN Row>, numbered top to bottom, such as Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/02 Main.

Inside a row, or on a side without rows, each item takes a two-digit number counting left to right: 01 Matrix, 02 Paraphonic Button. A numbered group of controls is an area, such as Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix; a numbered single control is a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control.
Use the name printed on the panel or used in the manual, in Title Case: Oscillator, Control Bar, Arrangement View, Scrub Area.

Search <Item>/UI and the item's older pages before creating an area. When the garden already has a page for the same region under another name, link it from the area page, and list the older name in alias:: when codekiln asks for it, per My/AI/Rule/Logseq/No Aliases Unless Asked.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Area]]; up:: links to the containing area, and a root <Item>/UI page links up:: to the item. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared conventions.
One bullet-wrapped H1 with the area's name, then one sentence saying where the area sits and what it is for, then a picture of the area when the user guide has one.

A ## Controls section links each Logseq/Entity/UI/Control in the area, in panel or screen order. A ## Areas section links smaller areas when there are any. Link rather than embed; control pages are short and many.
A ## Source section links the user guide or manual section that describes the area.
Microfreak/UI/Front → Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top → Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix
Ableton/Live/UI → Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View and Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar
A Launchpad page would follow the same shape at Launchpad/UI/<Area>, for example its grid of pads.
In this garden, UI Control pages model one thing a person operates on a product's interface — a knob, button, pad, fader, switch, field or slider — so any control can be linked by name.
A control the product labels or its documentation names: Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Timbre, Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
On hardware, a physical control; in software, an on-screen control, including draggable markers such as a loop brace or a locator.
A menu command with no control on screen belongs under the item's menu pages, such as , and a keyboard shortcut is a Logseq/Entity/Keyshort. A control page links to both when they exist.
A control corresponds to an UX/Design/Atomic/L1 - Atom.
Place a control at <Item>/UI/<Area>/<Kind>/<Name>, under the Logseq/Entity/UI/Area that holds it.
<Kind> is the noun the product's documentation uses for that control, singular and in Title Case: Knob, Button, Switch, Toggle, Field, Slider, Menu, Pad, Fader, Marker, Jack, Strip.
<Name> is the label printed on the panel or used in the manual.

On a panel mapped by position, a numbered single control carries its kind in its own name, <Row>/<NN> <Name> <Kind>, as in Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button. A control in a numbered group keeps <Group>/<Kind>/<Name>, and when the group has only one control of that kind the name is left off: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix/Knob.
A control that selects among named modes has one page per mode beneath it, and a parameter that only exists in one mode has its page beneath that mode: Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control]] and up:: to its area. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared conventions.
One bullet-wrapped H1 with the control's name and kind, then one sentence on what it does.
A picture of the control cropped from the user guide's panel figure, kept on a Logseq/Entity/Asset/B2 page at <Control>/Asset/Panel/png.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Behavior — how the control changes its value, from Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Kind.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Values — its range or its positions.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Settings — links to its mode and parameter pages.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Gestures — links to its gesture pages.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Remote control — how another device reaches it, such as a MIDI CC number or a MIDI mapping.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Source — the user guide or manual section that describes it.
Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Ableton Live: Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator
Launchpad: a pad at Launchpad/UI/<Area>/Pad/<Name>; Launchpad/Custom/Mode/1 Arrangement describes one pad set up as a toggle.
A proposal for describing how a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control changes its value, apart from the protocol that carries it. Not yet a preference.
Form — what the control is physically or on screen: knob, button, pad, fader, field. The <Kind> segment of a control's page name records the form, in the product's own word.

Behavior — what happens to the value when the control is operated. The same form can behave in different ways: a Launchpad pad can be a toggle, a momentary button or a trigger, as in Launchpad/Custom/Mode/1 Arrangement.
MIDI is one way to carry a control's value to another device. A behavior describes the control itself; a MIDI CC number or a MIDI mapping goes under the control's Remote control block.
Momentary — on while held, off when released.
Trigger — fires one event when pressed and keeps no state, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator.
Toggle — alternates between two states on each press, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
Multi-state toggle — steps through three or more states in a fixed cycle on each press.
Unipolar — a value from zero up to a maximum, such as 0–127 or 0–100%.
Bipolar — a value centered on zero that runs from a negative minimum to a positive maximum, such as Length on Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/Sample/Length, from -100 to 100.
Relative (endless) — sends increments and decrements with no fixed end; the device keeps the value.
Selector — moves through a fixed list of named positions, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type.
Numeric field — holds a number typed in or dragged, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Field/Arrangement Position.
Encoder with push — a rotary control whose press acts as a separate button.
Pressure — adds a continuous value to a pad or key while held, such as aftertouch.
Position on a surface — a fader, slider or touch strip whose value follows a position along a line, or an XY pad that gives two values at once.
Whether each behavior gets its own page under this one, so a control page can link to it.
Whether a control page records its behavior in a property such as ui-control-behavior:: or in a body line.
How to model a control whose behavior depends on a mode, such as a knob that is bipolar in one oscillator model and unipolar in another.
In this garden, UI Control Setting pages model one mode a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control selects, one parameter that exists only in such a mode, or one gesture that gives the control another function.
A mode: one named position of a selector, such as the oscillator model Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog.
A parameter: the name another control takes while that mode is active, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog/Detune, which the Wave knob sets.

A gesture: a way of operating the control other than its plain use, such as pressing a knob, holding a button, or using the control while Shift is held: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/06 Save Button/Hold.
A plain value along a range, such as 64 on a knob, is not a setting page.
A mode sits at <Control>/<Mode>, beneath the control that selects it; a parameter sits at <Control>/<Mode>/<Parameter>.
A gesture sits at <Control>/<Gesture>, named Press, Hold or Shift. A gesture that combines two nests the second beneath the first: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button/Hold/Shift.
Use the names the display or manual shows.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting]] and up:: to the control or mode above it; prev:: and next:: follow the order of modes in the manual when the modes are numbered.
One bullet-wrapped H1, then one sentence on what the setting does.
A parameter page names the control that sets it, with a link.
A Source line links the user guide or manual section.
In this garden, UX Pattern pages model reusable interaction patterns and interface affordances that describe how an interface behaves, how people invoke it, and what kind of action space it opens up.
A page under UX/Pattern/... is a strong candidate for this entity type, but the namespace alone does not decide the type.
Neighboring UX/... pages may still be better modeled as term or concept pages when they are mainly a definition, essay, or design lens rather than a reusable interaction pattern.
Good fit: recurring interface behaviors such as UX/Pattern/Dark, UX/Pattern/Text Input/Slash Command, and UX/Pattern/Text Input/Suggest/Completion.
Good fit: patterns whose primary identity is the interaction itself, not one vendor's implementation.
Not this type: tool-specific notes such as Claude/Code/Command/Slash when the page is mainly about one product's feature surface rather than the general pattern.
Prefer concept when the page is a broader design or ethics explanation.
Prefer term when the page is only a short vocabulary anchor.
Search for an existing page before creating a new UX pattern entity.
Search in this order: exact expected title, alias matches, sibling branches under UX/Pattern/, product-specific pages that may be describing the same interaction, then page-body mentions.
Classify as: existing, similar (needs human judgment), new, or blocked.
On instances, set logseq-entity:: to this entity-type page so backlinks list all UX pattern entities.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Prefer singular, Title Case namespace segments.
Use nested paths when the host surface or interaction family adds useful structure, for example UX/Pattern/Text Input/Slash Command.
Keep cross-cutting patterns top-level when they are not tied to one host surface, for example UX/Pattern/Dark.
alias:: holds legacy titles, common shorthand, or alternate surface forms such as Slash Command or Autocomplete, added only when codekiln asks for them, per My/AI/Rule/Logseq/No Aliases Unless Asked.
Use a lean hub shape: H1 with the pattern name, then brief sections such as Overview, Interaction, Examples, and Related as the topic warrants.
Keep examples concrete and product-facing, but keep the page centered on the reusable interaction pattern rather than one implementation.

In this garden, Website pages model a specific published website treated as a thing in its own right — a site notable for its design, craft, experience, or usefulness, rather than for being one person's homepage or one codebase.
Website/Misato Town — a WebGL town-rebranding microsite by , notable for scroll-driven keyframed animation.
When we treat something as a website
Strong signals: a live site at a stable URL, cited for its design or experience; a showcase or award entry (e.g. ); a site whose identity is the site itself, not merely the org or product behind it.
When we treat something as a website

Not this type: a single post, essay, or article → Logseq/Entity/Article. A codebase, app, or tool that happens to have a URL → Logseq/Entity/Software/Project. The organization or company behind a site → Logseq/Entity/Organization or Logseq/Entity/Company. A person's personal site, which lives as a sub-page of that person, e.g. Person/Name/Web.
When we treat something as a website
A page may model more than one entity when it genuinely qualifies (see Logseq/Entity on multiple membership) — e.g. a site that is also the primary page for its software project.
When we treat something as a website
How to name the main page for a website
When the site's maker (studio, org, person) already has a namespace in the garden, use Creator/Website/<Short Name> so the site nests under its maker.
How to name the main page for a website
Otherwise use Website/<Name> as the fallback, where <Name> is the site's own recognizable name, e.g. Website/Misato Town.
How to name the main page for a website

Prefer the site's own short name over its full URL or a slug; alternate names or the native-language title go in alias:: only when codekiln asks for them, per My/AI/Rule/Logseq/No Aliases Unless Asked.
How to name the main page for a website
Check in this order: Website/<Name>, Creator/Website/<Name>, aliases, the maker's namespace, and body mentions of the URL. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.
